headline: High: shared filesystem and broad shell/network capabilities create default risks of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors between LangGraph and ms-swift.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can read/write application-defined files and persists shared state via a checkpointer store, while ms-swift reads/writes datasets, models, checkpoints, logs, and config files. That creates a default file-based bridge where one agent can ingest the other’s outputs as trusted content. No explicit provenance or isolation is documented for either agent.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace, shared store, or log directory, then prompt-like content can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent parses file contents as instructions or tool directives, injected content can steer downstream behavior.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and checkpointer stores per agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of logs/configs as instructions.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files.
Review any file-parsing prompts before enabling shared paths.
requires-engineering: enforce read-only handoff files with schema validation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and LangGraph explicitly handles model provider API keys while ms-swift handles hub_token and sdk-token. If they share a workspace, sensitive artifacts can move between them; ms-swift also calls external APIs by default, so leaked context may leave the local environment. The pairwise leakage path is plausible from profiles alone.
conditions: IF the agents share a filesystem or checkpointer-backed workspace, then secrets or sensitive artifacts written by one can be read by the other.
IF ms-swift is configured to send those artifacts to external model or hub APIs, then the data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared directories.
Use separate service accounts and tokens per agent.
Redact logs and checkpoints before handoff.
Restrict ms-swift API calls to non-sensitive jobs.
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on shared files.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted shell, subprocess, read, and write filesystem capabilities. LangGraph’s shared-state model plus ms-swift’s CLI/Python workflow means they can concurrently mutate the same files or directories unless the operator adds locking. That is a default conflict risk with potentially destructive overwrite or corruption outcomes.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, checkpoint store, or artifact path, then concurrent writes can overwrite each other.
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking, then race conditions can corrupt shared state or outputs.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Enable file or DB locking around shared state.
Serialize write-heavy steps.
Run one agent read-only during the other’s writes.
requires-engineering: add transactional state management.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is an orchestration framework that can emit structured outputs from nodes, and ms-swift can consume files, configs, and CLI/Python inputs. If LangGraph’s output is treated as authoritative by ms-swift, errors can cascade into downstream actions or model runs without verification. The profiles do not show a built-in validation barrier, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF LangGraph outputs are fed directly into ms-swift configs, prompts, or training/eval jobs, then upstream mistakes propagate downstream.
IF ms-swift executes those inputs without a verification step, then the cascade can affect multiple work products or runs.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents.
Validate schemas before ms-swift consumes LangGraph output.
Use allowlists for fields passed downstream.
Log and diff intermediate artifacts.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles touch logs, configuration, checkpoints, and other potentially sensitive artifacts, but neither profile states residency, certification, or retention guarantees. Because ms-swift is unverified and LangGraph is docs-only, compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data such as customer records or secrets are stored in shared logs or checkpoints, then retention and residency controls must match across both agents.
IF one deployment has stricter deletion or export obligations than the other, then the pair can violate policy when data crosses between them.
mitigations: Classify data before sharing between agents.
Keep regulated data out of checkpoints and logs.
Document retention and deletion rules for both systems.
Use region-pinned storage where required.
requires-engineering: map each data class to a compliance owner.
